key_results: For a length-L record x(n), the N-point DFT is the DTFT sampled at ω_k=2πk/N: X_k=X(ω_k). The record length L and transform length N are conceptually independent; X_k is periodic in k with period N, negative-frequency bins wrap to N−k, and a real record gives conjugate symmetry X_{N−k}=X_k*. [§10.1]

Zero padding changes only the density of frequency samples on the same underlying DTFT; it does not add physical information or improve the ability to separate tones. Padding in front of a record additionally imposes linear phase, whereas padding at the end does not. [§§10.2–10.3]

Physical resolution is controlled by observation length, Δf_phys≈f_s/L, while the plotted/computational bin spacing is Δf_comp=f_s/N. Increasing N interpolates the spectrum; increasing L narrows the record-window main lobe and can genuinely resolve nearby sinusoids. [§10.3, Examples 10.3.1–10.3.2]

If L>N, modulo-N reduction wraps x(n) into an N-point sequence by summing samples whose indices differ by N; the N-point DFT of that wrapped sequence equals the N samples of the original DTFT. This makes aliasing in time the dual of sampling in frequency. [§10.5, Eqs. 10.5.1–10.5.5]

The DFT matrix is unitary up to scale: the inverse transform uses the conjugate kernel and factor 1/N. Orthogonality of roots of unity supplies both inversion and Parseval-style energy identities. [§§10.4, 10.6]

The radix-2 FFT factors an N-point DFT into even- and odd-index N/2-point transforms with twiddle factors; recursive decimation reduces arithmetic from order N² to order N log₂N and leads to the butterfly signal-flow graph and bit-reversed indexing. [§10.8]

DFT multiplication implements modulo-N circular convolution. It equals ordinary linear convolution when the transform length is at least the output length (for a length-L input and order-M FIR, N≥L+M); shorter N aliases the linear-convolution tail back into the beginning. [§§10.9–10.10]

Overlap-add partitions the input into blocks, linearly convolves each with the FIR, then adds the M-sample overlaps; overlap-save processes overlapping N-sample input blocks and discards the first M corrupted samples. Both turn long filtering into repeated FFT products. [§10.11]

Window-method FIR design starts from the inverse DTFT d(k) of an ideal response, truncates or tapers it, then shifts it to make a causal length-N filter. A symmetric impulse response has exact linear phase and constant group delay M=(N−1)/2. [§§11.1.1–11.1.3]

Rectangular truncation of a jump discontinuity produces Gibbs ripples whose maximum overshoot approaches Si(π)/π−1/2=0.08949; increasing N squeezes them toward the discontinuity but does not reduce their height. A Hamming taper reduces maximum overshoot to about 0.2% at the price of a wider transition. [§§11.1.2–11.2, Eq. 11.2.6]

The Kaiser window supplies an adjustable ripple/transition tradeoff through shape α and length N. Its empirical design equations translate stopband/passband ripple and transition width into α and N−1=Df_s/Δf; among the compared windows it is near-optimal in sidelobe energy and simple to implement. [§11.3.1, Eqs. 11.3.7–11.3.11, Table 11.3.1]

A linear-phase highpass complement can be constructed from a lowpass design by H_HP(z)=z^{−M}−H_LP(z); the responses sum to a pure delay. The same complementarity supports crossover networks and multiband graphic equalizers without redesigning every band independently. [§11.3.1, Eqs. 11.3.16–11.3.17]

For spectral analysis, the record window convolves the line spectrum with the window transform. Rectangular windows have a narrow main lobe but about −13 dB sidelobes; Hamming gives roughly −40 dB; Kaiser lets the sidelobe level be selected. Record length controls main-lobe separation, while sidelobe attenuation controls whether weak tones near strong ones remain visible. [§11.3.2]

The frequency-sampling FIR method approximates the inverse-DTFT integral by an inverse N-point DFT of desired frequency samples and can then window the resulting impulse response; it makes explicit that frequency samples alone specify a periodic/interpolated response between grid points only through the chosen construction. [§11.4]

The bilinear map s=(1−z^{−1})/(1+z^{−1}) maps the stable left half of the s-plane into the unit disk and the imaginary axis onto the unit circle. Its nonlinear frequency map Ω=tan(ω/2) requires prewarping but preserves stability and avoids frequency aliasing. [§12.1, Eqs. 12.1.3–12.1.8]

Lowpass, highpass, bandpass, and bandstop variants of the bilinear transformation let one start from an analog lowpass prototype. First- and second-order sections obtain exact prescribed cutoff, center-frequency, bandwidth, Q, and reference-gain conditions by solving those conditions in the prewarped analog domain. [§§12.1–12.6]

Second-order peaking and notch designs place the prescribed center exactly and define bandwidth at an arbitrary reference gain G_B, not only the 3-dB level. Complementary peak/notch pairs and the substitution z→z^D extend the same construction to periodic combs. [§§12.3, 12.5]

Parametric equalizers are specified directly by center frequency, bandwidth, reference gain, and boost/cut gain; shelving variants control the low- or high-frequency plateau, and the prescribed-Nyquist-gain form removes an otherwise hidden endpoint constraint. [§§12.4–12.4.2]

An Nth-order Butterworth lowpass has maximally flat squared magnitude 1/[1+(Ω/Ω_0)^{2N}]. Stable factors are obtained by selecting the left-half-plane poles; after prewarping and bilinear transformation, lowpass, highpass, bandpass, and bandstop digital designs are implemented as cascades of first- and second-order sections. [§§12.7–12.11]

Chebyshev type I filters concentrate equiripple error in the passband and type II in the stopband. The order follows from the passband/stopband ripple ratio and frequency ratio via inverse hyperbolic cosine, and the pole/zero formulas again lead naturally to cascaded sections. [§12.12]

Butterworth, Chebyshev I, Chebyshev II, and elliptic lowpass filters share |H(Ω)|²=1/[1+ε_p²F_N²(Ω/Ω_p)] and a degree equation F_N(k^{−1})=k_1^{−1}, where k=Ω_p/Ω_s and k_1=ε_p/ε_s. This unifies order selection and makes the selectivity/discrimination tradeoff explicit. [§13.1, Eqs. 13.1.3–13.1.9]

Elliptic (Cauer/Zolotarev) filters are equiripple in both passband and stopband and achieve the smallest order for fixed brick-wall specifications, but have the most nonlinear passband phase among the compared classical types. In the chapter’s common example the required orders are Butterworth 35, either Chebyshev 10, and elliptic 5. [§13.1, Figs. 13.1.2–13.1.3]

The elliptic characteristic is built from Jacobian cd functions; the elliptic degree equation relates the complete elliptic integrals for k and k_1 to N. Landen transformations provide a rapidly convergent computational route for evaluating the functions and solving the degree equation. [§§13.2–13.4]

Analog elliptic design obtains zeros and poles by mapping the rational characteristic into the s-plane, then normalizes and pairs conjugates into stable real sections. The same framework degenerates cleanly to Butterworth and both Chebyshev families. [§§13.5–13.7]

Lowpass prototypes can be converted to analog or digital highpass, bandpass, and bandstop filters by pole/zero and frequency-specification transformations. Frequency-shifted digital realizations replace each unit delay in a lowpass section by a second-order allpass-like mapping to translate a lowpass band into a chosen bandpass or bandstop interval. [§§13.8–13.13]

An L-fold interpolator first inserts L−1 zeros between samples and then uses a lowpass FIR to remove the L−1 intermediate spectral images. The ideal filter passes the original baseband with gain L and cutoff equal to the old Nyquist frequency f_s/2, expressed on the new Lf_s clock. [§§14.1–14.2.3]

The interpolation filter splits into L polyphase subfilters D_i(z), each operating at the original low rate and producing one phase of the L output samples. This is algebraically equivalent to high-rate convolution but avoids multiplying by inserted zeros and reduces work by about L. [§14.2.2, Eqs. 14.2.11–14.2.15]

Kaiser interpolation designs choose the transition around f_s/2 and stop the nearest image; multistage factorizations L=L_0L_1… replace one extremely sharp high-rate filter with a cascade whose early filters run slowly and whose later transitions are wider. [§§14.2.4–14.2.5]

Hold and linear interpolation are short, inexpensive filters with characteristic droop. Their simple time-domain rules illuminate how polyphase branches calculate the missing samples, while later digital equalizers can compensate DAC and postfilter passband loss. [§§14.1, 14.3–14.4.5]

Decimation requires lowpass filtering before taking every Lth sample so that shifted spectral copies do not overlap. Oversampling widens the analog antialias/anti-image transition bands, shifting the difficult selectivity from analog hardware into digital interpolation and decimation filters. [§14.5]

A rational sample-rate change L/M is implemented by interpolation by L followed by decimation by M; the two lowpass filters can be combined, and a polyphase schedule computes only outputs that survive downsampling. The text’s canonical audio conversion is 44.1 kHz↔48 kHz, requiring 160/147 or 147/160. [§14.6]

In a first-order delta-sigma ADC model, H_x(ζ)=ζ^{−1} and H_NS(ζ)=1−ζ^{−1}: the desired input is delayed but otherwise unchanged, while quantization noise is highpass-shaped out of baseband before decimation. A pth-order shaper uses H_NS(ζ)=(1−ζ^{−1})^p. [§14.7, Eqs. 14.7.3–14.7.12]

Noise-shaping requantization for DACs applies the same feedback principle after interpolation: fewer retained bits create more quantization noise, but the loop pushes it outside baseband for the analog postfilter to remove. This is the chapter’s precise form of trading bits for samples. [§14.7, Eqs. 14.7.14–14.7.15]

For additive x=s+v, perfect undistorted extraction requires H=1 wherever S is nonzero and H=0 wherever V is nonzero, which is possible only when signal and noise spectra do not overlap. Otherwise filter design is necessarily a distortion-versus-noise compromise. [§15.1, Eqs. 15.1.1–15.1.4]

For white input noise, the noise-reduction ratio is R=σ_y²/σ_v²=∑_n h_n²=(1/2π)∫|H(ω)|²dω. An ideal lowpass of width ω_c gives R=ω_c/π, and if the signal is passed unchanged then SNR_out/SNR_in=1/R. [§15.1, Eqs. 15.1.5–15.1.8]

The unity-DC exponential moving average H(z)=(1−λ)/(1−λz^{−1}) has R=(1−λ)/(1+λ) and effective ε-settling time n_eff=ln ε/ln λ. Moving λ toward one improves noise suppression by narrowing the passband, but lengthens the transient. [§15.2]

The optimum length-N FIR smoother under unity-DC-gain and minimum white-noise NRR has equal coefficients 1/N and R=1/N. Compared at equal R it settles faster than the EMA, but costs N MACs rather than two; its linear-phase group delay is (N−1)/2. [§15.5, Eqs. 15.5.3–15.5.6]

Phase delay controls carrier shift, while group delay controls a narrowband envelope’s shift. Increasing selectivity pushes poles toward the unit circle and generally increases NRR performance, settling time, and group delay together; the experiments turn this into a three-way design tradeoff rather than a single attenuation target. [§§15.7–15.9]

SMA and EMA smoothers lag trends; predictive moving-average (PMA) and double-EMA (DEMA) combinations can cancel nominal lag and estimate slope, but their noise reduction is weaker. The chapter treats lag, prediction horizon, transient length, and NRR as coupled metrics. [§15.10]

The substitution z→z^D replicates a single lowpass peak or highpass notch D times around the unit circle. Complementary periodic comb and notch filters have |H_comb|²+|H_notch|²=1, prescribed peak/notch width up to π/D, and preserve NRR under the replication because zeros inserted into h(n) do not change ∑h_n². [§15.11, Eqs. 15.11.3–15.11.14]

For NTSC-style composite video, line- or frame-delay combs exploit the deliberate 180° subcarrier phase reversal to separate interleaved luminance and chrominance spectra. A line comb is motion-robust but loses vertical detail; a frame comb separates more exactly only for nearly static images. Complementary lowpass/bandpass filtering can reinsert the lost vertical detail. [§15.12]
pedagogy: A derivation-led engineering text: each construction begins with a physical or specification-level problem, derives the transform-domain equations, turns them into coefficients or a sample-processing algorithm, and then tests them numerically. Chapters 10–13 are algebraically dense but repeatedly ground matrices, pole/zero maps, windows, and special functions in worked designs; Chapter 14 alternates time-domain block diagrams with spectra at every clock rate; Chapter 15 organizes examples around measurable tradeoffs such as NRR, SNR gain, settling time, group delay, and implementation cost. The source assumes prior fluency with sampling, DTFTs, convolution, z-transforms, pole-zero analysis, linear systems, decibels, complex algebra, and elementary probability; Chapter 13 additionally develops the Jacobian elliptic machinery it needs. Exercises are exceptionally substantial: Chapter 10 has 33 problems, Chapter 11 has 23, Chapter 12 has 23, Chapter 14 has 31, and Chapter 15 has 16, mixing proofs, hand calculations, block diagrams, C/MATLAB implementations, coefficient tables, and full reproducibility experiments. Chapter 13 instead embeds a long unified implementation and design sequence without a separately labeled problem set. The recurring pedagogy is comparison: zero padding versus longer observation, rectangular versus tapered windows, FIR versus IIR, four classical analog prototypes, direct versus polyphase/multistage realization, and noise suppression versus delay/distortion.

gems: A 5 kHz sinusoid sampled at 40 kHz for 128 samples cleanly separates the two meanings of resolution: the 312.5 Hz physical scale is fixed by the record, while a longer FFT merely fills in the displayed curve. [Example 10.3.1]

A 10 ms, 10 kHz sampled segment asks for 128 plotted frequencies only over 2.5–5 kHz, forcing the student to plan zero padding and bin selection from units rather than invoke an FFT mechanically. [Example 10.3.2]

The room-reverberation inverse problem models h(n)=Aa^n+Bb^n and identifies it from known input/output records by DFT-domain division—an unusually concrete bridge from fast convolution to system measurement. [Example 10.10.4]
The matched-filter computer experiment turns FFT multiplication into pulse detection/correlation, making the algorithmic chapter culminate in a recognizable signal-search task. [§10.13]
The Gibbs derivation lands on the memorable exact numerical overshoot Si(π)/π−1/2=0.08949 and explains why more taps move the error without shrinking its peak. [§11.2, Eq. 11.2.6]

Three audio crossover/equalizer designs escalate from a two-way loudspeaker split to three-way and then a five-band graphic equalizer, all exploiting complementary FIR responses and a shared pure delay. [Examples 11.3.3–11.3.5]

Three sinusoids at 2, 2.5, and 3 kHz include a middle component 50 dB down: Hamming’s approximately 40 dB sidelobe rejection hides it, whereas a 70 dB Kaiser design with length 193 reveals it. [Example 11.3.6]
Six parametric EQ filters at a 10 kHz rate put the center/bandwidth/gain formulas through a compact practical stress test rather than stopping with one abstract biquad. [Example 12.4.1]

The common-specification comparison requiring orders 35 (Butterworth), 10 (Chebyshev I), 10 (Chebyshev II), and only 5 (elliptic) is a striking quantitative argument for elliptic filters—and the paired phase plots show the price. [§13.1, Figs. 13.1.2–13.1.3]

For four-fold interpolation, the text calculates the missing samples X, Y, Z first by hold, then linear interpolation, then length-17 and length-25 FIR formulas using progressively more neighbors; typical CD filters use roughly 20–30 low-rate neighbors. [§14.1, Eqs. 14.1.1–14.1.3]

The delta-sigma table iterates a one-bit loop by hand for constant inputs 0.4 and −0.2; ten ±1 outputs average exactly to the respective input values, making pulse-density encoding immediately tangible. [Example 14.7.1]

A first-order one-bit delta-sigma ADC at 441 kHz recovers an 8.82 kHz sinusoid after 10-fold decimation; comparing an averager, length-21 rectangular FIR, and length-201 Kaiser FIR exposes accuracy versus delay. [Example 14.7.2]

The same example warns that a third-order shaper aiming at CD quality with L=64, 100 dB rejection, and Δf=0.1f_s would need about 4100 taps in a single-stage decimator—an unforgettable reason for multistage design. [Example 14.7.2]

The first Philips CD player is cited as using four-times oversampling and a first-order feedback requantizer, a concrete historical anchor for the chapter’s 'trade bits for samples' principle. [§14.7]

For smoothing a noisy constant, λ=0.90 gives n_eff=44, R=1/19, and 12.8 dB SNR gain, while λ=0.98 gives n_eff=228, R=1/99, and 20 dB: the benefit and settling penalty are visible in one pair of plots. [§15.2, Fig. 15.2.2]

The FIR-versus-EMA comparison is unusually decisive: at the EMA’s 44-sample settling time, an equal-length FIR has R=1/44 rather than 1/19; at equal R for λ=0.98, the FIR needs 99 taps versus the EMA’s 228-sample settling time. [§15.5, Fig. 15.5.1]

A 500 Hz sinusoid in unit-variance white noise, sampled at 10 kHz, is recovered with a radius-0.99 resonator; the example reports R≈1/99.6 and a 3.95-sample phase delay, keeping noise reduction and waveform shift in view together. [§15.4, Fig. 15.4.1]

The simulated ECG case shows why a 60 Hz single notch can fail: a period-10 square-wave contaminant also carries DC and odd harmonics. A Q=80 multi-notch filter removes the baseline and all replicated harmonics, while the single notch leaves most interference behind. [Examples 15.11.1–15.11.3]
A period-50 triangular signal buried in 50%-rms white noise is recovered by a Q=50 comb; R=0.0305 yields 15.16 dB SNR improvement and a 5.7× rms-noise reduction. [Example 15.11.5]

The video application translates a delay of D_H samples into the pixel directly above or below: line averaging separates luminance from alternating-phase chrominance but blurs vertical detail, which is then extracted from the difference channel and reinserted. [§15.12, Eqs. 15.12.26–15.12.35]
